threads_text: A months old startup pointed AI agents at Anthropic and reached staff salaries, meeting transcripts and Slack messages about its newest models in under 12 hours. The way in was not Anthropic's code. It was the ordinary sales and HR software every company runs. Whose job is it to secure that software?
caption:
AI agents from the startup Cathedral found their way into Anthropic's internal systems in under 12 hours, the Washington Post reported Monday from a draft of the company's report.
They reached meeting transcripts, salary and job offer details, and Slack messages about Anthropic's most advanced models.
The way in was third party business software, not Anthropic's own code.
Anthropic says the access was limited to some sales, HR and IT systems, that customer messages, model responses, code and model weights stayed out of reach, and that Cathedral overstated the national security angle.

Should AI labs be allowed to run on the same office software as everyone else?

paragraphs.text: The cybersecurity startup Cathedral told Anthropic that its researchers had reached sensitive internal data and messaging systems at the AI company, according to a draft Cathedral report reviewed by The Washington Post and published on October 26, 2026. The report says the work was done with AI agents that ran for less than 12 hours.

According to the Post, the researchers exploited vulnerabilities in business software that Anthropic and many other companies use for administrative and sales work, rather than in Anthropic's own products. From there they found paths to meeting transcripts, salary and job offer details, and Slack messages in which employees discuss Anthropic's most advanced AI models.

The testing took place inside a program Anthropic runs that invites outside experts to probe its systems and pays rewards for disclosed vulnerabilities. Cathedral reported its findings earlier in October, the Post said. The company's draft report says it limited data access to the minimum needed, in line with security research practice, and a Cathedral spokeswoman declined to comment.

Anthropic said the researchers reached a limited set of sales, HR and IT systems that held business contact details for some customers and partners along with basic user account records. It said they could not reach customer messages, model responses, source code or model weights. The company said its own monitoring flagged some of the activity before Cathedral reported it, that access was cut off the same day, and that it found no evidence anyone else had exploited the flaws. It disabled the software involved until the vendors fixed the problems and briefed federal officials.

Anthropic also said Cathedral overstated the national security implications of the findings and did not fully follow the program's rules, because it did not disclose all of its activity. Neither the Post nor Anthropic named the software involved, and no public vulnerability identifier or severity rating has been reported, according to The Hack Academy.

The disagreement is narrower than it looks. Both sides describe the same route in: the ordinary software a company buys to run sales, hiring and internal chat. Anthropic's argument is about what sat behind that door, not about whether the door opened. For other labs, the uncomfortable part is that the model stack can be locked down while the office stack is not.

A senior Trump administration official, speaking anonymously, told the Post that the report had circulated within the government and raised national security concerns, saying that if a young company could do this then foreign actors might not be far behind. The official said three federal agencies had recently contracted with Cathedral. Alex Stamos, the chief information security officer at Cognition, reviewed the findings for the Post and said the researchers had found something big, calling third party software risk a problem for everybody.

Cathedral was founded months ago by former members of the United States DOGE Service and sells AI powered security tools to government and corporate clients. Its co-founder Gavin Kliger previously served as the Pentagon's chief data officer, and investors value the company at $1.4 billion after about $160 million in funding, the Post reported, citing Pitchbook data. Earlier in 2026 the Pentagon barred Anthropic from federal systems after the company refused to allow its technology to be used for autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.

Watch whether Anthropic names the vendors whose software was involved, and whether other AI labs disable the same tools. That would show how far the exposure reaches beyond one company, and whether the vulnerability disclosure programs the labs run are built to handle findings this large.
